newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Lev/mark peg seen boosting Bulgarian ties with EU.
newsitem.headline: Lev/mark peg seen boosting Bulgarian ties with EU.

text.p: Bulgaria's interim cabinet's proposal to peg the lev to the mark as anchor currency in a fixed exchange rate regime will link its economy closer with the European Union in the long term, officials said on Monday.

"It is best for Bulgaria to conform its currency board to the major currency of the European Monetary Union to be set up in 1999," Financial Stabilisation Council member Ventsislav Antonov told reporters.
The council advising the interim cabinet on Monday recommended the mark as an anchor currency but the final decision is to be taken by parliament and the new cabinet to be appointed this week.
Prime minister designate Ivan Kostov is expected to present his cabinet lineup to parliament on Wednesday.

With Germany now Bulgaria's biggest investor and trade partner, the bulk of foreign investment is expected to come from Europe and it is necessary to create favourable conditions for it, said Antonov.
"This is also a way to synchronise the rhythm of our economic cycle to that of European economies," he added.
Traditionally the dollar has been perceived as benchmark of stability as people convert their savings mostly into dollars.

Dollar trade accounts for around 45 percent of the domestic forex daily turnover and the lev exchange rates for other major currencies are adjusted to their spot rates against the dollar on international markets.

Under a $548 million 14-month standby agreement sealed with the IMF, Bulgaria pledged to introduce a self-regulating restrictive monetary mechanism, known as a currency board, in a bid to stabilise its shaky financial system.

Under the currency board system the lev will be pegged to an anchor currency, at a rate that will be set by the government and parliament in the week of the system's introduction and will not be adjusted.
The Bulgarian National Bank's fixed mark/lev rate for Monday was 912.14.
An International Monetary Fund mission is in Sofia to help draft legal amendments needed to make the board operational.

"The psychological effect of this proposal sought by the stabilisation council is to prompt people to convert their savings into marks and thus return their mattress money to the banks," said economist Krassen Stanchev, director of the Institute for Market Economics.
Around $1 billion was withdrawn from banks in the past year after a chain of bank failures shook the financial system, economists say.

"It is a natural decision. Most of the currencies in the region shadow the mark and transactions in marks will increase," said Christos Katsanis, Balkans Regional Director of the National Bank of Greece. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
